persons.name: Bora Özkent
persons.digest: In this Sunday video he explains how to build a one-person business in the AI era. He recommends turning a skill into a product that solves a clear problem for a specific customer and systematizing the research, content, product, sales and support steps. Against the 'it won't work in Turkey' pessimism in the comments, he asks viewers to stay optimistic and says honest money-making is possible.

items.title: Build a One-Person Business, AI at Your Service!
items.summary: Continuing last week's video on four income mechanisms, he explains how to build a one-person business. He says it starts with a skill that is narrowed into a product solving someone's specific problem. Using photography as an example, he recommends covering five areas: research, content creation, product creation, sales and customer support. He notes customers buy results rather than features and says he talks in terms of benefits for his Haddini Aş club and terminal. He says an offer should have four elements, including the result and the way to reach it. He stresses using AI as a tool that speeds up processes rather than as a pure programmer. He says social media is the main tool for reaching customers. He urges viewers not to give in to the pessimism that it can't be done in Turkey or only with connections, and says earning honestly is possible.

persons.name: Defiant Gatekeeper
persons.digest: He calls the week flat: the **S&P 500** fell about 0.3% and the **Nasdaq** rose about 0.5%, but the focus remains the US 10-year yield, which ranged between 5.18% and 5.34%. He says the Treasury's $6 billion buyback was already priced in and that Cayman funds hold a record of more than $460 billion in Treasuries as of July. He describes the Fed repeating its inflation stance via Kashkari and Cook, and France's 2027 budget pushing the OAT-Bund spread above 85 bps. He says September payrolls of 29k, below expectations, lifted equities, reflecting a 'bad is good' mindset.

items.title: Volatile yield and France...
items.summary: He summarizes the week in five topics. The S&P fell about 0.3% while the Nasdaq rose 0.5%; the 10-year yield ranged between 5.18% and 5.34%. First, the Treasury's $6 billion buyback: he says its impact was limited because it was announced in advance. Second, Cayman Islands funds holding a record of more than $460 billion in Treasuries as of July 2026, which he reads as macro hedge funds doing basis trades trying to lock in yields. Third, the Fed: he relays Kashkari's and Cook's messages that victory on inflation cannot be declared and that they are ready for more tightening if needed. Fourth, France's 2027 budget with €25 billion in cuts and higher corporate taxes; the opposition threatened a no-confidence vote, the France-Germany 10-year spread exceeded 85 bps, and he says political stability is what matters most. Fifth, September nonfarm payrolls of 29k against 89k expected and unemployment at 4.2%, with the Nasdaq rising about 1.2% on Friday. He takes this as proof the market fears the Fed's rate path, and that inflation drives rates, rates drive the 10-year yield and the yield drives equity valuations.

assets.note: Closed the week down about 0.3%.
Closed the week up about 0.5%; rose about 1.2% on Friday.

persons.name: Berk Dinçtürk
persons.digest:
He argues that with the **S&P 500** and **Nasdaq** at all-time highs, bond yield and oil headlines are not wrecking the economy; he says tech will lead into year-end and that **Micron**, **Dell**, **Nvidia** and **QQQ** can be considered. He has closed his **Russell 2000** position and recommends taking profits. Citing Judy Shelton's appointment to the Treasury advisory board, he says he has no reservations on **gold** and **silver**; he says the Treasury could step in if the 10-year yield heads to 5.5%, which would be a buying opportunity.

In a separate video he recommends focusing on the crypto theme for the rest of the year and coming years: **Bitcoin**, **Ethereum**, **Solana**, **Coinbase**, **Robinhood**, **Circle** and **Strategy**, but with a time horizon. In Q&A he says he still likes **Tesla**, has not held **SoFi** for 5-6 months, likes **Lumentum** and holds **Energy Fuels** long term.

items.title: Investment Strategies in Times of Uncertainty | Berk Dinçtürk
items.summary: He says bond yields and oil have not wrecked the economy despite the headlines, and that the 10-year yield staying at 5.20-5.30% while the US economy grows strongly is not a disaster. He notes oil has hovered around $100 for months, Iran misplayed its Hormuz card, and the US began selling reserves at $114. On inflation data, he claims the statistics agency changed weights and compares it to the Arthur Burns era. He says profitable tech will lead into year-end and that Micron, Dell, Nvidia, QQQ and Lumentum can be considered; he has closed his Russell 2000 position and recommends taking profits. He says that if the 10-year yield heads to 5.5% the Treasury could intervene, and that the resulting correction would be a buying opportunity for those without index exposure. Citing Judy Shelton's appointment, he says his view on gold and silver is unchanged, noting silver fell from $120 to $60 but that one should wait. He still likes Tesla and has not held SoFi for 5-6 months. On energy, he holds Energy Fuels long term because of the VAC acquisition and the Mesa project and sees it as a $50 company. On crypto, he says Bitcoin and Solana held up while the market wobbled and may run first on the rebound.

It says Micron's >35% revenue coverage under long-term agreements through 2030 could prove conservative, with Asian peers above 50%.

assets.note: Long-term agreement coverage above 35%; JPM thinks it may prove conservative.

items.title: TSMC and Terafab talks
items.summary: Reports Elon Musk confirmed talks between TSMC and Terafab on chip manufacturing in Texas, including TSMC possibly using Terafab as anchor customer for a future fab, but said they are just discussions.

assets.note: In talks with Terafab on Texas cooperation; Musk says 'just discussions'.

items.title: Stock screening filters
items.summary: He rules out market caps under $300 million, insufficient liquidity, EPS growth under 10% a year, no catalyst to carry growth, lagging the sector and market, weak institutional interest, companies running out of cash that may not find financing, and dilution. He says a big fall does not make a stock cheap, that he doesn't have to catch every opportunity, and shares his Finviz screen.
